name: Enterprise World Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: The superleague belt the CSWA staged as its own top prize between the Unified Championship's tours. Mike Randalls won the sixteen-man founding tournament over Flic Rair at BATTLE OF THE BELTS X in November 1994 and lost it five weeks later to the Muppet Maneuver and a downed referee; Tom Adler escaped a double-title cage with it in August 1995, Randalls took it back on sixty points in the CSWA X-MAS IRONMAN CHALLENGE, GUNS powerslammed him for it in the SuperPRIMETIME triangle on Martin Luther King Day 1996, and Mark Windham left WINTER'S WARRIORS VII with it after Hornet turned on GUNS and a paid-off referee counted the fall.

name: Enterprise World Tag Team Championship
epitaph: A tag championship the CSWA ran alongside its Unified belts for a single documented year. Generation X-Press won the EN World/US tag tournament final over the FORCE at BATTLE OF THE BELTS XIV in July 1996; the Japanese Assault took it from Troy Windham with the Shogun Slam in a unification match at FISH FUND XI that September, and the fed's own record carries nothing further.

name: Greensboro Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: A promotion naming a championship after the city it was invented in, and then defending it for thirteen years. Big Wesley Slack won the founding tournament in 1988; Mark Windham took it from him and then retired it when he won the CSWA Heavyweight Championship, and Jay Youngblood was defending it again by 1989. It goes dark for years and comes back: the fed's own newspaper records Aaron Douglas as the first Greensboro Champion since 1997 when he beat Apocalypse in the tournament final at ELVIS LIVES XI in January 1999. From there it moves fast — Randy Harders, Douglas again, Blade, Wicked Sight, Sky Suicide, Evan Aho — and the fed's own Champions page still has a holder for it in April 2001.

name: Greensboro Tag Team Championship
epitaph: The fourth belt of 1988 and the shortest-lived in the fed's own record. Strange But True won the founding eight-team tournament, beating Ace In The Hole in the final on the fourth card of the year, and lost it the next year in a belt-against-belt match with the United States Tag Team Champions. Nothing after that survives.

name: CSWA Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: A second singles belt, made in 1988 alongside the World Championship and gone from the fed's own record long before the web. Purple Hayes won a tournament for it on the third card of 1988; Ed Parsons took it from him on the fourth and Mark Windham took it from Parsons on the fifth, retiring the Greensboro Championship when he did. Vladimir Rushevcof beat Berserker for it in 1989. After that the fed's own archive stops carrying it and its Champions pages never list it again.
notes: Distinct from the World Championship, which the same 1988 cards track separately: on the fifth card of 1988 Mark Windham wins this belt while Joey Melton defends the World Championship in the main event.

name: Intracontinental Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: Named in the fed's own founding memoir as one of the belts added over the years, and surviving in exactly one document: the CSWA's own Champions and Contenders page on PRODIGY, updated 15 July 1997, which lists it as vacant and to be decided in an eight-man tournament. No champion for it appears on any page held here, before or after.

name: CSWWA Ladies Enterprises World Championship
epitaph: A women's championship crowned once in the surviving record: Queen Sonya beat "Stone Cold" Stephanie Conner in the tournament final at FISH FUND XI in September 1996 to become its first holder.

name: CSWA Presidential Championship
epitaph: A belt tangled up with the office it is named for. The fed's own newspaper describes it as previously retired and revived at THANKSGIVING WEEKEND SPECTACULAR '99, when a returning Co-Commissioner ousted the other one from the commissionership and put the title back on a wrestler. Randy Harders lost it to a returning Alex Wylde in an impromptu match in Philadelphia; Aaron Douglas took it from Cameron Cruise at ANNIVERSARY 2000 on a three-count made by Hornet himself. By April 2001 the fed's own Champions page carries it as vacated, to be filled at ELVIS LIVES XII, and does not say why.

name: ULTRATITLE
epitaph: The tournament trophy the CSWA invented and then leased out across the hobby, first run on PRODIGY in 1992 with sixty-four entrants and by 1995 seeded to two hundred and fifty-six men across four divisions. Dr. Silver beat Timmy Windham with the Suicide Machine in the 1995 final at WINTER'S WARRIORS VI; the 1996 edition put its winner, Paul Pierce, straight into the Unified World Championship.

name: Unified World Tag Team Championships
epitaph: The fed's own tag championship after the merges, carried by two men rather than renamed for each of them. Eddy Love and Kevin Powers won it at BATTLE of the BELTS XVI in May 1999; by December 2000 the fed's Champions page has Foreign Exchange holding it, and by April 2001 Simply Stunning, since PRIMETIME in Paducah. The fed's own page writes it plural — Championships, two belts — throughout.
notes: The fed's own Champions page header reads "Unified World Tag Team Championships", plural. Whether and how it descends from the 1988 CSWA World Tag Team Championship is not settled by any page held here.

name: United States Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: One of the three belts the fed built in its first year, and the one that changed hands most. Jay Youngblood won the founding tournament in 1988 and lost it to Hornet on the very next card; Safari Sakan took it off Mark Windham in 1989 and Windham won it straight back. Eleven years later it was still the belt a run got built on: Kevin Powers won a tournament for it at FISH FUND XII in 1998, Eli Flair took it in a Triangle match in January 1999, and Nemesis won it twice in the same year, the first time out of a Barbed Wire Ladder Match he came into with a concussion. Lawrence Stanley and Havoc carried it through 2000.

name: United States Tag Team Championship
epitaph: Made in 1988 out of an eight-team tournament the Big Connection won, beating Armed and Dangerous in the final. By 1989 the fed was staging it belt-against-belt with the Greensboro Tag Team Championship, and the Overseas Connection beat Strange But True in that match. The fed's own archive carries it no further.

name: CSWA World Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: The first belt the CSWA made, and the one it kept. Joey Melton is defending it on the second card of 1988 and Hornet takes it from Purple Hayes the year after; a decade later it is still the fed's own main event, won out of an eight-man tournament at FISH FUND XII in August 1998 and carried through steel cages and IRONMAN round-robins until the record thins out. Its 1999 is the year that reads hardest: Hornet wins it in San Antonio in April and is stripped of it by a Co-Commissioner at BATTLE of the BELTS XVI, Eli Flair takes the vacancy out of the ANNIVERSARY IRONMAN, and Deacon takes it from Flair at THANKSGIVING WEEKEND SPECTACULAR and holds it for most of a year. The fed's own Champions page ends that reign with a sentence it does not explain further: the title was relinquished, in November 2000, on a diagnosis. It was still being defended on the board in 2004.
notes: Called the CSWA World Championship on the 1988 and 1989 cards and the CSWA World Heavyweight Championship on the Champions pages from 1998; the same belt throughout.

name: World Six-Man Championship
epitaph: A six-man belt the fed created in its first year and put on its own three lead characters: Joey Melton, Hornet and Mark Windham took it by beating the Big Connection and Purple Hayes on the second card of 1988. The fed's founding memoir lists it among the titles added as the game grew, alongside the Intracontinental, the Pacific and the Eastern States Heritage; of those four, this is the only one the 1988 card archive actually crowns anybody for.
notes: The memoir names Intracontinental, Pacific and Eastern States Heritage championships alongside this one; no card held here crowns a champion for any of the three, and only the Intracontinental turns up again, listed vacant on the fed's own 1997 PRODIGY Champions page.

name: CSWA World Tag Team Championship
epitaph: The first tag championship, and the one act that runs through the whole of the fed's first two years. The C.S. Express beat the Big Connection to become the first champions in 1988 and then defended it on every card the archive lists: a lumberjack two-out-of-three falls against the Dirty Duo, a double bullrope match against the Indian Warriors, a scaffold match against Armed and Dangerous. They were still holding it at the end of 1989.

name: PRODIGY Unified World Championship
epitaph: Not one federation's belt but the whole board's, and the CSWA is where its record survives. It began as the CSWA's own Unified Championship, built up across 1992 by Hornet challenging the champions of the other leagues in the Enterprise Superleague, and on 24 October 1993 the IRONMAN of CHAMPIONS at the CSWA's LAST CALL II merged the IWCCW World, the AAWC World and that ten-title CSWA belt into one. Over the next three months Hornet added the UWL Superleague's half and the AR Superleague's title to it. It was retired and re-won twice — a sixteen-man tournament in 1994 that ended with a masked man unmasking himself as Mark Windham, a 128-man ULTRATITLE in 1996 that made Paul Pierce champion — and by 1997 the fed's own page describes it as more than forty championships merged into one and sanctioned by PRODIGY. A five-member committee decided its matches on votes for roleplay quality. Mike Randalls won the last of it on 21 January 1997, the last reign the CSWA's own ledger records. A different fed's broadcast, New Frontier Wrestling's own Wrestlebowl II a decade later, separately bills the same-named belt in a comedic "Monkey Championship Wrestling" interlude — Professor Tremendous, already champion, pinning the last of three billed monkey challengers and unifying it with three more belts. No document joins the two readings; both stand.
notes: Filed under the CSWA because the CSWA is where it started and where its ledger survives; the belt itself was contested across the PRODIGY Wrestling BB's own federations and administered by the Unified Championship Committee, not by the CSWA alone.
